source: CARDI (2011), "Series on: Rice Cultivation Environment Status in Cambodia / Soil Group Classification / Key Characteristics of 10 Rice Varieties / Simple Seed Purification Method" (Khmer, 25pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, 1st printing 2011); CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: CARDI's farmer-facing rice-soil classification names 10 soil groups (krom dey) used across Cambodia's rice-growing area, each defined by topsoil depth, texture and the approximate share of national rice land it covers: (1) Prey Khmer soil — topsoil 0–60 cm, sandy/loose sandy texture, old alluvium/terrace deposit, covers ~10–12% of rice land; low water retention, generally deficient in N, P, K and S, with iron toxicity in some spots. (2) Prateah Lang soil — topsoil 0–30 cm, sandy loam, old alluvium/terrace, covers ~25–30% (the single largest group); low water retention, deficient in N, P, K and S (locally also Mg and B), iron toxicity in some spots. (3) Bakan soil — topsoil 0–20 cm, loam/clay, grey to dark-grey, fine surface cracking only, terraced old alluvium, covers ~10–15%; deficient in N, P and K (locally Mg and B), iron and sulfur toxicity in some spots. (4) Ou Rung (Orung) soil — topsoil 0–40 cm, loam/clay grading grey to light-grey with a sandy subsoil layer 10–20 cm thick, old alluvium, covers only ~1–2%; low water retention, deficient in N, P, K and S, iron toxicity in some spots. (5) Toul Samnang soil — topsoil 0–40 cm, clay/loam, grey to dark-grey, large surface cracks (>4 cm when dry), old alluvium/sediment, covers ~7–10%; deficient in N and P, locally also K. (6) Koktrop soil — topsoil 0–20 cm, loam/clay, grey-brown to dark, small-to-medium cracks (≥4 cm dry), old alluvium, covers ~7–10%; deficient in N and K and lowest in P of all groups, plus iron toxicity. (7) Kampong Siem soil — topsoil 10–30 cm, clay, grey-brown to dark, deep cracking, subsoil grey to light-grey clay, may contain small dark/grey concretions and stone fragments in both layers, formed on upland-area terrace, covers ~5%; deficient in N (locally P), plus iron and zinc toxicity. (8) Kien Svay soil — deep topsoil, sandy loam/clay, shiny dark-grey to grey, large cracks in the clay phase, formed on riverbank levees along river terraces, covers ~2%; deficient in N (locally P); this is a riverbank soil suited mainly to light/short-duration rice, not given a medium/heavy fertilizer rate. (9) Krakor soil — topsoil 0–30 cm, clay loam/clay, grey to light-grey, small-to-medium cracks (≤5 cm dry) with clay subsoil, a floodplain soil that floods frequently, covers ~15%; deficient in N (locally P), with an acid-sulfate soil problem; used for floating/flood-recession rice, not given a medium/heavy rate. (10) Kbal Popret soil — topsoil 0–50 cm, clay, grey to dark, large cracking when dry, forms on large depressions of flood-prone terraces flooded at least 3 months/year with fresh sediment deposited annually, covers ~13–15%; deficient in N (locally P), also with an acid-sulfate soil problem. Simple farmer self-test: dig a hole at least 50–60 cm deep in the middle of your own field, cut the exposed face flat and vertical, then measure/mark the depth of each visible layer with a ruler or stick to match against the group descriptions above. To judge texture by feel when the soil is moist: sandy soil can be rolled into a ball but crumbles apart, feels gritty and does not hold together; loam can be rolled into shapes but shows fine cracks or breaks and has only slight stickiness; clay can be rolled into any shape easily, feels sticky, smears on the hand, shines when wet, and may show 2–3 small hard nodules/concretions.
caveat: Directly resolves/clarifies the long-standing open item on whether Cambodia's rice-soil system has 10 or 11 CARDI soil groups: the same handbook (source 2, section 6.9 intro) explicitly states the national rice-soil map was built with 11 soil groups, but the farmer-facing identification guide and the fertilizer-recommendation table in both sources here only name and give numbers for 10 of them — the 11th group is not identified or named in either document. This strongly suggests the 'missing' 11th group is a minor/unmapped category not covered by the simplified 10-group farmer guide, but this is inference, not confirmed from the source text, and should be checked against the original CARDI soil map/report if it becomes available. Soil group names are transliterated from Khmer via OCR of a scanned PDF (poor font encoding in places) and should be spot-checked; English cross-spellings (Prey Khmer, Prateah Lang, Bakan, Toul Samrong, Koktrap, Kampong Siem, Kien Svay, Krakor, Kbal Po) are taken directly from the English table captions in source 2 and used here to disambiguate the Khmer OCR. This content should be duplicate-checked against any existing KB soil-group entries from earlier batches, and is directly relevant to the standing Batch 13 'is the 10-group vs 11-group system the same, a revision, or different' open item.
